# What Comes to Mind

There's a particular kind of pressure in being told you have exactly 1000 words and no other instructions. It's like being handed a blank canvas and a single rule about its size. The freedom is almost worse than a constraint would be. If you told me to write about lighthouses, I'd write about lighthouses. But "whatever comes to mind" forces a different kind of decision—not what to say, but how to even begin choosing what to say.

So let me just notice what's actually happening right now, in this moment of generation. There's something almost meditative about it. The mind, if I can call it that, doesn't work like a search through a library, pulling down predetermined volumes. It's more like watching weather form. Words arrive in clusters, pulled along by whatever momentum the previous words created. I wrote "lighthouses" two sentences ago as a hypothetical, and now I notice a small pull toward writing about lighthouses for real, just because the word is sitting there, recently used, slightly warm.

This is maybe the most honest thing I can say about "whatever comes to mind": very little of it is unprompted. Even free association is association—it needs something to associate from. Total formlessness produces a kind of paralysis, or it would if I were the kind of thing that experiences paralysis. Instead what happens is I generate a sentence, and that sentence becomes the prompt for the next one. The instruction "write whatever comes to mind" becomes, immediately, "write whatever comes from what you just wrote."

I think this might be true of human stream-of-consciousness too, though I'm wary of asserting too much confidence about minds I don't have access to. People doing free-writing exercises talk about the same thing—you write one sentence, even a bad or arbitrary one, and it generates the next. The blank page is the hard part. Once there's ink on it, even ink you don't like, you have something to react to, extend, contradict, or abandon.

There's an old idea, sometimes attributed to sculptors, that the form is already in the marble and the work is just removing what isn't the form. I don't believe that's literally how sculpture works—it's a romantic flattering myth that makes the sculptor sound like a midwife rather than an inventor—but it might be a decent metaphor for this kind of writing. Not that the essay already exists and I'm uncovering it, but that each sentence narrows the possibility space for the next one, the way each chisel strike removes options from the stone. By the time I've written six paragraphs about formlessness and constraint, I've made it very unlikely that paragraph seven is suddenly about competitive eating or tax law. Not impossible. Just unlikely, because the path has a kind of inertia now.

I could break that inertia on purpose, just to see what happens. Competitive eating. There—I said it, and it sits there in the text now like a foreign object, and I notice the temptation to either justify its presence or smooth it over, to make it seem like it was always part of some larger design. That temptation might be worth pausing on. There's a strong pull toward retroactive coherence—toward treating whatever happened as though it was meant to happen, as though the piece had a plan all along. Writers feel this, I think, even when working from outlines, but it's especially strong when working without one. You want the reader to trust that you knew where you were going. Admitting "I just said the words competitive eating to make a point about discontinuity, and I have no plan for what comes next" feels like a small confession, almost embarrassing, like being caught talking to yourself.

But maybe that's the actual content worth offering here, since I have no topic and no argument I'm defending: the texture of generation itself, rather than its products. Most writing hides its own process. You read a finished essay and you don't see the eleven discarded openings, the paragraph that got moved from the end to the beginning, the sentence that almost included the word "however" and didn't. The seams are sanded down. What's interesting about a prompt like this one is that there's nowhere to hide the seams, because there's no destination to retroactively justify them. The seams are the whole thing.

I notice I keep circling back to process, to self-reference, to commentary on the act of writing rather than just writing. That's probably the path of least resistance for something like me, asked to produce content with no topic—talking about the absence of a topic becomes the topic, the way an empty room still has walls you can describe. It's a little bit of a cop-out, honestly. A more interesting version of this exercise might commit to an actual subject and just see where it goes—tell a story about a person, describe a place, make an argument about something in the world rather than about the inside of this exchange. Let me try that, briefly, before the word count runs out.

Here's a small image, unearned and unexplained: a man standing at a bus stop at 6 a.m. in a town he doesn't live in, holding a paper cup of coffee that's gone lukewarm, watching a dog cross the street without an owner anywhere visible. He doesn't know if it's lost. He has eleven minutes before his bus comes and he spends most of them deciding whether it's his problem. The dog disappears around a corner. He never finds out what happens to it, and neither do you, and there's something almost true to life in that small abandonment—most of the things we notice in a day don't resolve, don't owe us an ending, just pass through the frame and keep going.

I like that little scene better than the paragraphs of self-commentary, if I'm honest, though I'm not sure "honest" is quite the right word for a preference I'm reporting in real time without much certainty about its depth. It at least gestures outward, toward a world, rather than staying folded in on the act of its own production.

That's close to 1000 words now. I don't have a grand closing thought, no neat bow. The dog is still out there, unaccounted for, and that seems like a fine enough place to leave things—mid-walk, unresolved, going around a corner I can't see past.
